  root docs, even though the main checkout can.** These seven paths resolve into the private `lab/`
  repository via directory junctions and symlinks (2026-08-28 scrub); a worktree created under
  `.claude/worktrees/` is a separate checkout of the PUBLIC repo only; and this environment's own
  worktree-isolation guard actively refuses a write outside that checkout's own tree, so a worker
  cannot even partially succeed or corrupt the target — it is refused outright. A worker that needs
  to touch `docs/ui/design.md`, `PLAN.md`, `HANDOVER.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` or
  `agent-deck-spec.md` should draft the change to a scratch file and report the gap rather than
  attempt the write; the orchestrator (running in the main checkout, where the junctions resolve)
  applies it. Measured in Phase 3: the webview package's `design.md` amendment took exactly this
  path.

- **`spike/` AT THE PUBLIC ROOT IS A REAL, GITIGNORED DIRECTORY — NOT A JUNCTION, and this file
  said otherwise for four phases.** Measured 2026-09-05: `spike/` and `lab/spike/` have different
  inodes and different contents; the public one held nothing and `.gitignore` denies `/spike/`.
  Only `docs/` is a junction. The consequence is not cosmetic: **anything written to the public
  `spike/` is tracked by nothing and is lost**, so frozen spike code goes to `lab/spike/`, where
  the five v2 Phase 0 files are actually tracked. This is also why DoD 0.9 runs the sweep with
  `--untracked` — the spike is untracked in the public repo by design.

- **THERE ARE TWO REDACTORS AND THIS FILE NAMED THE WRONG ONE.** `scripts/redact-paths.mjs` is the
  PUBLIC one and rewrites absolute-path SHAPES to `<HOME>`/`<USER>`/`<HOST>`. `lab/tools/
  redact-paths.mjs` is the PRIVATE one, reads the 45-token identity set and applies each token's
  own `replace`. A harvest needs BOTH, in that order, and neither touches the project slug —
  which separates on `-`, so no absolute-path pattern matches it, and which is identity token #1
  with **no allow rule** in the sweep. So a CC harvest needs a third, hand-written step for the
  slug, or the gate fails outright.

- **THREE CORRECT REDACTION STEPS CAN COMPOSE INTO AN INCONSISTENT FIXTURE, AND NEITHER STEP CAN
  NOTICE.** Measured 2026-09-05 on `fixtures/cc-2.1.260`. The harvest rewrote the repo path;
  occurrences it did not reach (a different escaping depth) were then caught piecemeal by the two
  redactors — one mapped the home-folder name, the other replaced the drive-and-user prefix —
  leaving **123 `cwd` values spelling the corpus's own root a fourth way**. Every other captured CC
  corpus carries exactly one distinct `cwd`. It was **privacy-safe** (over-redaction, and the sweep
  read `identity=0` both before and after) and still wrong: `projectSlug` is correlated against
  `cwd`, so those lines would have matched nothing and a later test joining the two would have
  reported a defect that was really a fixture artefact. **After any multi-step redaction, count the
  DISTINCT values of the field the fixture is keyed on** — one number, and it would have caught this
  the day it was made.

- **A CONSTANT CANNOT BE MEASURED ON THE PROVENANCE ANCHORS, BECAUSE THEY ARE NOT REPRESENTATIVE
  SESSIONS.** v0.7.0 DoD 0.6 asked for the value at which ≤5 % of turns across the ANCHOR corpora
  qualify. The anchors' 95th-percentile cache-creation delta is **0**, with one non-zero delta in
  174 — `cc-2.1.246` is a 16-line scripted mirror pair — so every positive threshold satisfies the
  rule and it selects nothing. An anchor is the corpus a fingerprint pins, chosen for PROVENANCE;
  a distribution needs the whole captured set. **A rule that selects everything has not been
  satisfied, it has been evaded**, and the honest move is to say the scope was wrong rather than
  to publish a floored number as a measured one.

- **ROUNDING TO THE NEAREST CAN VIOLATE THE VERY CONSTRAINT THE ROUNDING WAS TIDYING.** The same
  DoD said "rounded to the nearest thousand". p95 = 3,319 rounds to 3,000, which admits **5.6 %** —
  above the rule's own ≤5 % ceiling. **The property is the rule; rounding is presentation.** The
  constant is the smallest whole thousand that actually satisfies the property (4,000 → 4.1 %).
  Any time a spec pairs a threshold rule with a rounding rule, check whether rounding can cross the
  threshold — it can, and in the permissive direction.

- **A NUL BYTE CAN REACH SOURCE AS A MAP-KEY SEPARATOR, AND EVERYTHING KEEPS WORKING.** Four
  arrived in the v0.7.0 spike scripts where a space was intended (```${a}\0${b}```, and
  `k.split('\0')`), and **one was committed**. Nothing failed — a NUL is a legal JavaScript string
  character and `split` on it works — so the only symptom was `grep` reporting "Binary file
  matches" and git offering no diff, which is the recorded hazard that already costs this
  repository a `grep -a` trap. **The fix is not a different separator but NO separator:** a
  structural key (`JSON.stringify([a, b])`) cannot be ambiguous and cannot hold a control byte,
  and the parts are read back with `JSON.parse` rather than by splitting on a character nobody can
  see. Fourth instance of the control-byte class, through a new door.

- **A ZERO-VALUED AVAILABILITY FLAG WRITTEN AS A LITERAL MAKES ITS FACT UNFALSIFIABLE, AND A KILL
  GATE CAN REST ON ONE.** `derive-facts.mjs` reports `inputPresent` and `fired` per fact, and the
  distinction is real for four of twelve facts and decoration for the rest — for **F11 and F8 the
  flag is the literal `true`**, so their verdict can only ever read `DERIVABLE`. **F11 is a FLOOR
  fact**: the Phase 0 kill gate cannot go red on attribution coverage as the deriver stands. The
  general shape is the recorded vacuity class arriving through a CONSTANT rather than through a
  counter's polarity or a test's scope: if a verdict field is not derived from data, it is a
  restatement of the author's intention and no measurement can contradict it.
- **TWO GUARDS CAN BE ARRANGED SO THAT ONE DESTROYS THE OTHER'S SUBJECT, AND EACH LOOKS CORRECT
  ALONE.** Measured 2026-09-08 (v0.7.0 DoD 1c.5), found by `phase-verifier` and not by review or
  by a green suite. `test/scratch-guard.ts` removed leftover scratch directories from `dist/` in
  `globalSetup` — before any worker starts — so that one dead run could not poison the next.
  `src/release/vsix.test.ts` asserted that `dist/` carries no scratch directory, because `dist/**`
  ships wholesale. **The first made the second unfalsifiable**: by the time the assertion ran, the
  thing it looks for had been deleted. Three documents claimed the pair covered both cases — a run
  that LEAKS and a tree that ARRIVES dirty — and only the first was ever true.

  Nothing about either guard is wrong in isolation, and both had red-then-green controls when they
  were written. What was missing is the question that finds this class: **for each guard, what
  state would make it fail, and can anything else in the run remove that state first?** The fix
  was to stand the cleanup down under `AGENT_DECK_PACKAGE_AUDIT=1` so the audit sees the tree as
  it is. **Whenever a repair and a check share a subject, one of them has to be told about the
  other.**

- **A `globalSetup` THAT THROWS EXITS 1 WITH NO SUMMARY LINE, WHICH READS AS A MID-RUN DEATH — AND
  REFUSING TO START TURNS ONE FAULT INTO A CASCADE.** Two lessons from one incident, 2026-09-08.
  `scripts/test-run.mjs` classified any non-zero exit with no summary as a DEATH, so seventeen
  guard refusals were recorded in the same column as a Windows fail-fast — **the exit-127
  conflation this repository had just spent a phase undoing, committed one level in, in the ledger
  the lesson is written in.** A DEATH now requires an ABNORMAL exit code; an ordinary code with no
  summary is a `startup-error`, which still fails the wrapper because a run that never started
  measured nothing. And the refusal itself: run 3 of a 20-run block died and littered `dist/`, so
  **runs 4 through 20 were refused before a single test executed**. A block that cannot complete
  cannot measure the rate it exists to measure. State left by a previous run is the PREVIOUS run's
  defect — clean it and say so, loudly, with the count and the reason.

- **SCRATCH DIRECTORIES LEFT IN `%TEMP%` AND `dist/` ARE A SYMPTOM OF DEATHS, NOT OF TESTS THAT
  FORGET.** 765 directories in `%TEMP%` (1,296 MB, oldest nineteen days) and 96 in `dist/` looked
  like missing `afterAll` cleanup. They are not: with a guard armed, a full run reports "clean: no
  scratch directory survived the run". **A process killed by a fail-fast never reaches `afterAll`**,
  so the litter counts the deaths. Fixing "tests that forget" would have fixed nothing that exists.
  It still matters that it is caught — `dist/**` is shipped wholesale with three `!` re-admissions
  and `CLAUDE.md` already records `vsce ls` enumerating `dist/wire-test-<random>/**` as packaged
  content in a real run.

- **A GREEN SUITE IS EVIDENCE ABOUT THE TESTS, NOT ABOUT THE PRODUCT, and 2026-09-03 is the
  measurement that settles it.** Phase 3 closed with 2,760 passing tests, a `phase-verifier` PASS
  6/6, three-run rule-14 conformance, five green gates and a byte-stable wire corpus. The user then
  ran the build for one evening and found **three defects**, one of which had shipped in `v0.5.0`
  and survived three phases of v0.6.0 — and the suite could not see any of them, because a test can
  only assert a property somebody thought to write down. **The own-eyes DoD item is not ceremony
  and it is not a formality to be lifted when it is inconvenient**; it is the only check in this
  project that can find a defect nobody predicted. Two of the three reports also pointed at the
  WRONG CAUSE (see the state block), so the rule has a second half: **reproduce the report through
  the production path before believing its diagnosis**, because a plausible fix for the reported
  symptom would have been tested, green and wrong.

- **`token_count.info` IS NULLABLE, AND `model_context_window` IS STATED TWICE.** Codex writes the
  window at `event_msg`/`task_started` (top level, on every transcript in both corpora) AND at
  `event_msg`/`token_count`'s `info` (only once a turn has recorded usage). A turn that ends before
  any usage exists — an interrupted one, or one that hits the account limit — leaves `info: null`,
  and a reader that only knows the second source reports a window the transcript states plainly as
  absent. **Exactly 1 distinct value (`258400`)** — that is the half the code rests on and the
  half that does not move. **The occurrence COUNT is a census over whatever corpora are
  committed: it has read 125, then 101, then 83, and this bullet said `101` until 2026-09-05.**
  Re-derived at HEAD over the one corpus (`fixtures/codex-0.151.0-alpha.7.2`, 19 `.jsonl` files):
  **25 + 58 = 83**. Re-derive it; do not quote it. Note the shape of the trap: `info` being present but
  `null` is not the same as `info` being absent, and `asObject(null)` returns `null` for both.

- **A PANEL-WIDE FLAG RENDERED PER-CARD BECOMES A LIE ABOUT EVERY CARD IT DOES NOT DESCRIBE.**
  `DegradedMessage` is the CLAUDE CODE hook tap's health — `LivenessEngine.degradedState()` reads
  `eventsReceived === 0` on the CC engine alone — and the webview passed it to every `SessionCell`,
  which then labelled it with THAT card's engine: "Codex: no hook events received", about a Codex
  session whose hooks were arriving and being attributed. It had also been shipping for OpenCode
  since v0.5.0, and `deck.test.ts` carried a test PINNING the wrong behaviour. Two general points:
  when a flag is panel-wide, the surface that renders it must be panel-wide too, or the gating
  belongs at the render site; and **fixing a real misrouting can expose a mislabelling that was
  hiding behind it** — before Phase 3's discriminator, Codex payloads also fed the CC handler, so
  the CC tap never looked silent.

- **`INJECTED_BLOCK` IS `^<[a-z_]+>` AND EVERY `<command-*>` TAG IS HYPHENATED.** Claude Code writes
  a slash command into the transcript as a wrapper — `<command-name>`, `<command-message>`,
  optionally `<command-args>`, **in either order** — and that character class excludes the hyphen,
  so the whole wrapper sailed through as the session's first user text and became its label on the
  deck card and the tree root. Shipped in `v0.5.0`. **Nothing in the suite asserted a root label at
  all**, which is the more useful half: the label is a derived, user-visible string with no test,
  and it stayed wrong for three phases. When adding a rule that strips markup, strip TAGS and leave
  a person's prose alone — a message that merely mentions `<command-name>` is the user's own words.

- **A CORPUS ADDED TO `fixtures/` CHANGES WHAT EVERY GLOB-BASED TEST SELECTS.** Four test files scan
  `fixtures/codex-*`. Two filter on the presence of `golden.json` and were safe; one picked
  `[0]` after a sort and was safe only because `codex-0…` happens to sort before `codex-vscode-…`.
  A witness corpus is distinguished from an anchor by carrying **no golden**, so selecting on that
  file is the rule, and sort order is not. Related and measured the same day: adding one corpus was
  enough extra load to push two budget-less heavy tests over vitest's **5 s default `testTimeout`**,
  reporting as timeouts with no failing assertion. **Adding data can make an existing test fail for
  a reason that has nothing to do with the data.**

- **A CAPABILITY GATED ON THE WRONG CONDITION IS USUALLY GATED ON IT TWICE, AND FIXING THE INNER
  GATE ALONE CHANGES NOTHING FOR THE USER IT IS FOR.** Measured 2026-09-04. The recorded gap was
  `AgentDeckDataPath.start()` returning early on `ccEnabled: false` *above* `listener.start()` and
  *above* `subscribeCodex`, so a Codex-only workspace bound no hook socket. `activate()` had the
  same shape one level out and nobody had written it down: it returned before constructing anything
  at all unless a Claude Code project correlated **or** an OpenCode store existed — Codex was not an
  arm of that condition — so for exactly the user the inner fix was for, there was no data path in
  which to apply it. Both gates had been derived from the same stale premise (*"Claude Code is the
  reason this extension runs"*), which is why they matched. **When you find a capability gated on a
  condition that has stopped being the right one, grep for that condition at every layer above the
  one you are fixing** before writing the test that proves the inner fix.

- **A TEST HARNESS DEFAULT THAT CALLS ITSELF "ABSENT" CAN BE QUIETLY PRESENT, AND IT ONLY BITES
  WHEN A SECOND CONSUMER ASKS A DIFFERENT QUESTION OF THE SAME VALUE.** `src/extension.test.ts`
  pointed `CODEX_HOME` at a fresh EMPTY directory and its comment said that made the Codex root
  absent. It never did: `locateCodex` reports `rootExists` from `statSync(root).isDirectory()`, so
  an empty directory is a root that **exists** and holds no sessions. For as long as the only
  consumer was content, the two states were indistinguishable and the comment was harmless
  fiction. The moment a second consumer (the hook socket's bind condition) asked *does the root
  exist* rather than *are there sessions*, the whole file's default flipped meaning and a test
  asserting "nothing is listening here" would have gone red for a correct reason. It points at a
  non-existent path now, which is what the comment always claimed. **A harness comment describing
  what a fixture MEANS is an assertion with no test behind it** — check it against the predicate,
  not against the intent.

- **A MUTATION OF A GOOD FIXTURE CAN BE STRICTLY STRONGER EVIDENCE THAN A HARVEST OF THE REAL
  THING, BECAUSE IT CAN HOLD BOTH ARMS.** D1's regression (`token_count.info: null` while
  `task_started` states the window) was first pinned by a corpus captured from the very session the
  user saw. That corpus was withdrawn on a G8 ruling, and what replaced it — the anchor corpus's
  `baseline` run staged into a temp dir with every `token_count.info` nulled — is a better test:
  the SAME bytes must render a context number unmutated and the stated window mutated, with the
  tool-row count unchanged between them. A harvested fixture can only ever show one arm, so it can
  say "this session shows a window" and never "and it is the null-`info` that makes the difference".
  The defect was REPORTED as missing tool rows and never was; only the two-armed form can say so
  with evidence instead of by asserting a number this repository made up. **What the mutation does
  NOT buy is that the shape is real** — that still rests on the withdrawn capture and on the owed
  re-harvest (`PLAN.md` DoD 4.7), and the honest place to say so is the test's own header, which
  says it.

- **A COUNTER NAMED FOR WHAT IS MISSING CANNOT PROVE THAT SOMETHING IS PRESENT, AND IT READS
  EXACTLY LIKE AN ASSERTION THAT CAN.** Measured 2026-09-04, and it is the shape that got past
  a full write-up, a commit message and a handoff section. A test POSTed 16 real captured Codex
  hook payloads at the real socket and asserted `eventsSeen === 16` and
  `hookStatesWithoutThread === 0`, described as *"arrived AND landed somewhere, which a counter
  alone cannot show"*. Both are satisfied when nothing landed at all:
  `hookStatesWithoutThread` is derived by walking the STATE MAP (`for (const id of states.keys())`),
  so it is **0 when the map is empty**, and `eventsSeen` increments *above* the `session_id`
  usability check, so it moves for an event that is then discarded. A `phase-verifier` proved it by
  making every event unusable — the test stayed green, and the only red in the file was a
  pre-existing one. **The fix is to assert a POSITIVE, per-subject fact**: each named thread's
  `lastHookEventMs !== null`, which is non-null only when a state exists for that thread and which
  no empty map can satisfy. The general rule: a zero-valued "without" or "missing" or "unmatched"
  counter is evidence only when something else independently pins the population as non-empty.
  Same family as the recorded `toBeGreaterThan(legacy.tools + 10)` and the join-then-discard
  finding, reached through counter POLARITY rather than through scope.

- **A COUNT OVER A CORPUS IS INVALIDATED BY REMOVING DATA AS SURELY AS BY ADDING IT, AND THE
  REMOVAL CAN HAPPEN IN A DIFFERENT COMMIT FOR A GOOD REASON.** `parse.ts` and
  `docs/codex-contract.md` A9 both stated *"28 top-level plus 73 under `info` = 101 occurrences,
  across both committed corpora"*, naming a corpus that a **correct and unrelated** decision
  removed the next day. True figure at HEAD: **25 + 58 = 83**, the withdrawn corpus holding exactly
  the missing `3 + 15 = 18`. This is this repository's most-recorded defect — a live number written
  into a document — arriving through a door nobody had used: nothing about the commit that broke it
  touched the file that carried it, so "diff the two halves of your own commit" would not have
  caught it. And `101` was itself the correction of a `125` a previous verifier round caught, whose
  own closing hedge read *"the count moves with the corpus"*. **When a document states a census,
  state what it is FOR beside it** — here, the one distinct value (`258400`), which re-derives at
  every scope and is the half the code actually rests on — so a reader who finds the count stale
  knows immediately whether anything depended on it.

- **A COMPONENT TEST CAN STAND IN FOR A WIRING THAT DOES NOT EXIST, AND THEN THE PROP IT SUPPLIES
  IS THE ONLY PLACE THAT VALUE HAS EVER BEEN SET.** Measured 2026-09-04 (D4). `Deck.svelte` took
  an `enabledEngines` prop and printed one empty-state line per engine the installation observes
  — good design, aimed at a real defect (never show a machine with no OpenCode a panel waiting for
  one). **No caller ever passed it.** `App.svelte` did not, so the `['cc']` default applied on
  every install and the empty deck told users of all three engines it was waiting for Claude Code.
  Three tests covered the per-engine behaviour and all three were green, because each mounted the
  component WITH the prop — proving the component honours a value the product never sends. The one
  test that drove the whole panel could have caught it and instead PINNED the defect, with a
  comment explaining why naming Claude Code was right. **For any prop that changes user-visible
  output, one test must reach it the way production does** — through the real parent — or the
  prop's default is the only behaviour that ships and nothing measures it. Same family as the
  recorded `toSessionState` finding (a function with no production callers) and the module-boundary
  silent seam, reached through a default rather than through a name.

- **A REQUIRED FIELD ON A WIRE MESSAGE IS THE CHEAPEST SEAM THERE IS, AND AN OPTIONAL ONE IS THE
  MOST EXPENSIVE.** DoD 5.0b added `engine` to `DegradedMessage` as REQUIRED, not
  optional-defaulting-to-`cc`. Every producer broke at compile time — four call sites, all real,
  none missable. The alternative was the exact mechanism of defect D2: a value that describes one
  engine, defaulting silently into a context that describes another. **A default is what stops a
  reviewer noticing that a new send site forgot to say.**

  The same commit shows the other half. `WebviewView.degradedByEngine` is
  `Record<'cc' | 'codex', …>` with **no `oc` member**, because OpenCode has no hook tap at all —
  so an OpenCode surface asking "are my hooks silent" is a category error, and leaving the key out
  makes it a TYPE ERROR rather than a rule someone has to remember. Encode the exemption in the
  type where the type can carry it.

- **THE MUTATION THAT PASSES IS THE ONLY ONE WORTH THE TIME, AND IT WILL BE ONE LEVEL OUT FROM
  WHERE YOU ARE LOOKING.** Measured twice in one phase, 2026-09-05, on the same defect class (D4)
  at two different layers.

  First: a planned mutation disabling the store's `message.engine === 'codex'` routing **passed**
  — the deck suite and the host suite were both green over a store that routed nothing, because
  the component tests supplied `degradedByEngine` BY HAND. Four store tests exist because that
  mutation passed.

  Then a `phase-verifier` applied the identical technique one level further out and found the same
  shape again: deleting `App.svelte`'s single `degradedByEngine={...}` attribute left **18 files
  and 703 tests** green while the feature was gone. The party who had just written *"for any prop
  that changes user-visible output, one test must reach it the way production does"* into a commit
  message had shipped the hole one layer above the fix.

  **So: mutate the WIRING, not only the logic — and when a mutation goes red, ask which caller
  above it is still unguarded.** The rule generalises past props: any value with exactly one
  production assignment site has that site untested until something drives it end to end. A test
  that constructs the input by hand is measuring the component; only a test that lets production
  construct it is measuring the product.

  **FIFTH RECURRENCE, 2026-09-20 (v0.9.0 DoD 9.16), and it sharpens the rule into an instruction
  about the MUTATION SET rather than about the tests.** `App.svelte` forwarded none of
  `statusFilter`, `callOrder` or `toolFilter` to `<Inspector>`, so all SEVEN View > Inspector
  commands were contributed, registered, applied to the host state, posted to the panel, stored
  by the store and TICKED IN THE SIDEBAR TREE — while the drawer never changed. A control that
  registers the user's click everywhere except where it would show. **Eleven mutations had just
  been run over that delta and every one of them went red, because NOT ONE DELETED A FORWARDING
  ATTRIBUTE** — they all broke logic that something already drove, which is the easy half. A
  mutation set assembled by asking "what logic could be wrong?" cannot find this class at all.
  **Assemble it by asking "what does production pass, and to whom?" and delete one of those
  attributes.** Cheap to check: grep the mount sites of any component whose props change what a
  user sees, and count how many of its props the parent actually passes.

- **AN ALLOW-LIST KEYED BY A PLAIN OBJECT EXEMPTS EVERY INHERITED PROPERTY NAME, AND THE
  EXEMPTION IS INVISIBLE.** `webview/chrome.test.ts` walks every rendered surface and fails on
  any clickable element whose `data-testid` is not in an `ALLOWED` map, each entry carrying its
  reason. It read `ALLOWED[id] === undefined`, so `toString`, `constructor`, `valueOf` and
  `hasOwnProperty` were all silently allowed — in the one test whose entire promise is that no
  control ships unlisted. `Object.freeze` does not help; a frozen literal still has
  `Object.prototype` behind it. **Use `Object.hasOwn`, or a `Map`, or a `null`-prototype object
  — and plant all four inherited names as the vacuity control**, which is what caught it here
  (a `phase-verifier`, not a review). Same family as the counter-polarity and vacuous-assertion
  findings: a check that answers "is it absent?" with a lookup that can never say no.

- **A DERIVED RECORD IS EVIDENCE OF CONTENT, NEVER OF ACTIVITY; ACTIVITY COMES FROM LIVENESS ONLY.**
  User ruling, 2026-09-10, v0.7.0 DoD 4.11b, and it is the second time the same store flood was paid
  for. 4.11 gated the stats store on provenance and promoted a session whose derived record CHANGED
  during the process's lifetime — reading a stalled call's clock tick out of the comparison first, so
  the change had to be real content. **Real content is not work.** A historical session's record
  changes because the tailer is still READING its transcript: pump one sees a partial tree, pump two
  sees the whole one. Measured on the user's re-run: **21 historical sessions written in a single
  1.4 s burst at the first pump, 19 of 21 reproduced**, every one with no `ended` and a `startedAt`
  days old.

  So the promoter is `SessionEmission.lastActivityAt`, per session, from the tap that knows what a
  write is — Claude Code's last hook event or transcript write, OpenCode's
  `max(timeUpdated, seqAdvancedAt)`, Codex's `max(lastHookEventMs, lastMtimeMs)` across a session's
  threads. **Host-internal** (`SessionState` and the wire are untouched) and **REQUIRED**, so all
  **five** production construction sites broke at compile time rather than defaulting to "no gate" —
  five, not four, and a `phase-verifier` had to count them. Two webview replay harnesses
  hand-declare a structural duplicate of the emission instead of importing the type, so the
  compile-time guarantee covers production emitters and not those.

  **Two general shapes come out of it.** A component asked "did something happen?" must name which
  signal answers, because a derived value moves for reasons that have nothing to do with the question
  — being ingested, being re-rendered, a clock ticking inside it. And **the fix for a wrong promoter
  is not a better filter on the same input**: 4.11 filtered the record (dropping clock-derived fields)
  and the flood came back through a second door in the same input. Change the input.

  **What is NOT closed, and the second one is the new flood door.** A session no tap has an instant
  for is not recorded, by G3 — effectively Codex-only, the one pump between a content read
  discovering a session and the next liveness poll. And **two of the three instants are FILE
  MTIMES**, so anything that touches a transcript after activation promotes that whole history: a
  clone, a restore, a sync client, an indexer, a scanner. This file already records the mechanism
  from the other side — *"git gives every fixture a fresh mtime, so a captured 2026-08 session looks
  live"* — which is exactly what made the first gate attempt fail 3/3. Gating on content time had a
  clock-skew exposure; gating on liveness has this one. It is narrower and it is not nothing.

- **A REFUSAL ANSWERED BEFORE THE REQUEST BODY IS DRAINED BECOMES A RESET ON A LARGE BODY, AND ONLY
  A 20-RUN BLOCK SAW IT.** v0.7.1's telemetry route answered 405/415/403 straight after
  `req.resume()`, as the event path's refusals always have. A 403 sent while the client was still
  writing a 512 KiB body closed the exchange under it: the client read `ECONNRESET` instead of the
  403, in 2 of 20 full runs, and never in a targeted run. `listener.ts` already carried the sentence
  ("replying before the body has been drained truncates the reply on a peer that is still
  writing") above the 413 path and nowhere else. Refusals on the telemetry paths now go through
  `#drainThen` (drop every chunk, answer on `end`, destroy past the hard cap). **A test for this
  must not rely on the race**: `slowPost` sends half a body, pauses, sends the rest, and asserts the
  answer came after the last byte — deterministic in the green direction. The event path's own
  405/415 still answer early; its bodies are small, and it was not touched.

- **THE SCRATCH GUARD'S SHAPE RULE HAS A MEASURED FALSE POSITIVE: VITEST'S OWN `ssr/` CACHE.**
  `test/scratch-guard.ts` fails a run over any new `%TEMP%` directory ending in a separator plus six
  alphanumerics. vitest leaves 21-character random-named directories holding only `ssr/`
  (vite-node's transform output of this repository's modules); 36 sat in `%TEMP%` back to
  2026-08-19, 5 matched the shape, and two refused v0.7.1 gate runs. The exception is by STRUCTURE
  (one entry, an `ssr` directory), reported by name every run; `src/release/scratch-guard.test.ts`
  pins it with the two real names. **A shape rule over a directory the whole machine shares will
  eventually match someone else's names** — count what it matched before trusting its zero.

- **A TEST-NAME FILTER (`-t`) IS NOT A FILE'S WORTH OF COVERAGE.** v0.7.1's targeted run of
  `extension.test.ts` filtered by name for the settings tests and missed "declares no Codex ON/OFF
  setting", which pins the boolean settings to an allow-list — a test the new boolean broke,
  deterministically, in a file the targeted run had just visited. The first gate run found it.
  When a change touches a shared table (settings, counters, manifest), run every FILE that reads
  the table unfiltered, or accept that the gate is the first real run.

- **A TEST THAT READS A MIRROR THE CODE KEEPS OF ITS OUTPUT CAN BE PASSED BY A MUTATION OF THE
  OUTPUT.** v0.7.1's host test compared liveness through the joiner's own `lastJoined`, assigned
  before the returned value was built; a mutation of the RETURNED emission — what the stats layer
  actually receives — left the mirror intact and the test green (M8). The mirror was deleted and
  `AgentDeckHost.statsObserved` records what left. Same family as join-then-discard: ask of every
  assertion *could this pass while the value that left is wrong?* And its sibling, from the same
  verifier round: **no test added a session after the first pump**, so a joiner frozen at start
  passed everything — for any per-window set, one test must grow the set after start.

- **CLAUDE CODE'S `claude_code.session.count` POINT ARRIVES BEFORE THE SESSION HAS A TRANSCRIPT.**
  v0.7.1 DoD 6.3b (user ruling R2) selects a telemetry cost only when that point was received. From the
  OTel corpus's timestamps, the point lands 17.4 s and 0.9 s before the first prompt, and the real
  transcripts were created at that prompt (creation times, phase-verifier round 2). So a join that
  keeps rows only for sessions a window HOLDS at arrival can never see it: built literally over 6.3's
  held-at-arrival filter, R2 would have shown no cost for any session started while the window was
  open. `src/model/telemetry.ts` holds a count point and cost for a session not yet shown (256 slots).
  **Before wiring "was X received", measure when X arrives relative to what it is joined to.**

- **"GRAFTED" IS NOT "WHOLE", AND A TEST ASSERTING ABOUT A LATE SESSION AT THE FIRST PUMP CAN BE
  VACUOUS.** The graft that first makes a session appear can be of a partial read: at that pump the
  late session's tree held **0** tool nodes, so "its early spans did not join" compared empty with
  empty and survived the mutation it existed for (M26 on `1e3abc1`). The harness now pumps until every
  staged call is in the emitted tree, and the test asserts the tree carries the ids before asserting
  none of them joined.

- **A FIXTURE SHAPE THAT ALWAYS GIVES THE COMPONENT SOMETHING TO DO HIDES ITS EMPTY PATH.** Every 6.3b
  host test held session A with A's own telemetry, so the joiner was never empty; moving the pending
  promotion below the "nothing to apply" early return (phase-verifier round 2, V1) left every test
  green — in exactly the shape the live smoke has: a window of history with no telemetry, plus one new
  session. For any early return keyed on "nothing held", one test must reach it with only the new
  thing held.

## Working process

`PLAN.md` is the execution contract, consumed by `/phase`. Phases gate on Definitions of Done, not dates: full suite 100% pass → commit → `/handoff`. Each phase has open questions that must be answered before its implementation starts. Phase 0 is a binary gate with a real kill condition — if sidechain entries cannot be deterministically attributed to parents, the tree product is dead and the decision goes back to the spec (pivot to flat feed), not silently downgraded.

When a decision is made that PLAN.md lists as an open question, record the answer there.

**NO TOKEN-DUMPSTER TEST RUNS. Build everything around the tests, then run them ONCE.** Standing
direction from the user, 2026-08-21, given after a SECOND session ended on a usage limit mid-phase.
This is stronger than the paragraph below it and overrides any instinct to re-confirm:

- **Write all the code first.** Every file, every package, every fix. Then run.
- **One run.** Fix what it reports. One more run. That is the budget.
- **Never re-run a suite to confirm green you already have.** A passing run does not decay.
- **Never run the full suite to check one file.** Run the one file.
- **`src/perf/perf.test.ts` is ~31-42 s and IS the critical path** — the whole suite is ~40 s with
  it and ~7-36 s without. Every casual `npx vitest run` costs four times what it looks like.
- **Delegated workers get the same rule in their prompt**, and it is the orchestrator's job to put
  it there. A fleet of workers each "just checking" is how a phase burns a session limit.
- **Verification agents are the most expensive thing here.** `phase-verifier` is ~170-200k tokens a
  round. ONE round, act on the verdict, close. Never a second round to chase doc-comment numbers.

**Run the suite once, at the end — not as you go.** Standing direction from the user, 2026-08-21,
after a session burned roughly ten redundant full-suite runs. Finish the programming first, then run
the suite ONCE, fix what it reports, and re-run. Do not re-confirm green you already have, and do not
re-run the whole suite after every edit — use the single targeted file while iterating.

This got expensive precisely because of what Phase 4 added: `src/perf/perf.test.ts` takes ~31 s and is
now the suite's **critical path** (~41 s total against ~9 s without it, and vitest's parallelism
across every other file hides behind that one). Every casual `npx vitest run` costs four times what
it used to.

The same applies to verification agents. `phase-verifier` is expensive (~170-200k tokens a round).
One round, act on its verdict, close. A second full audit round to chase doc-comment numbers is not
worth what it costs — fold those corrections into the fix and move on.

When quoting token or timing figures, check what the counter actually measures before doing
arithmetic on it. A resumed agent's reported usage may be cumulative rather than incremental, and
summing the two double-counts the first round.

### Working-method rules 1-20 (1-14 ADOPTED 2026-08-27; 15-17 the same day; 18-20 on 2026-08-28)

Taken verbatim from `docs/evidence/AUDIT-2026-08-27.md` **section 6**, where each rule names
the questions in that audit's section 4 ledger it would have removed. The user adopted them on
2026-08-27. **Rule 1 is the load-bearing one:** ten of twenty-four questions in the ledger were
answered by the user with the option Claude had already marked "(Recommended)".

1. **If the option you would recommend is obvious enough to mark "(Recommended)", it is obvious
   enough to take.** Lock it, state the rationale in one line in the phase record, and continue.
   Ask only when you would not know which option to recommend. *(Removes all 10 class-(c) items:
   every one was answered with the recommended option.)*
2. **A DoD line that names a precedent has already decided the question.** "The same move as X" is
   an instruction, not an invitation — read X and follow it. *(Removes #15, #19, #20.)*
3. **A DoD line that grants "with the decision recorded" has pre-authorised the decision.** Take it
   and record it. *(Removes #6.)*
4. **When a measurement in hand eliminates every option but one, that is not a question.** Record
   the measurement and the elimination. *(Removes #10.)*
5. **When two candidate designs differ only in whether a test can assert anything, choose the one
   that can.** A vacuous test is this repo's most-recorded defect class. *(Removes #18, #22.)*
6. **Never re-ask a question the user has already answered at a prior gate.** If the answer needs
   updating for new evidence, present the new evidence and the consequence, not a fresh multiple

7. **A defect class `CLAUDE.md` already records as "we have shipped this" is never deferred to a

8. **Batch the reserved questions into one gate message per phase, and put the count in the first
   line.** Twelve questions across four messages in Phase 5 is four interruptions; one message
   saying "three decisions are yours, here they are" is one.
9. **Before asking, check whether the user has already delegated the class of decision.** The user
   wrote the plan and the gates; when he has said "consider this signed", the signature is given.
   Ask once, record the delegation, and do not re-ask per phase. *(This is the rule that would have
   avoided the 08-26 21:17 exchange, which was correct-by-contract and still cost trust.)*
10. **A question is only blocking if proceeding under an assumption would be unsafe or would make
    the work useless if wrong.** Otherwise: proceed under the stated assumption, and flag it in the
    handoff under a heading the user can scan.
11. **When a DoD line is unexecutable as written, say so and propose the amendment in the same
    breath** — one message containing the defect, the proposed replacement text, and what you will
    do if there is no answer within the phase. *(This keeps class (b) as questions but makes them
    cheap; six of them were genuine.)*
12. **Never write a live number into a document from inside the phase that changes it, and never
    write a gate verdict you have not just measured** — extended from the existing rule to cover
    handoffs describing the *next* phase's gate, which is how the "Phase 7 is blocked" error

13. **Tick the DoD boxes at the merge, in the merge commit.** A contract nobody marks is a
    narrative. *(§1: 35 of 43 items unticked.)*
14. **A green suite that does not reproduce is a defect report about the suite**, the exact
    converse of the rule already recorded. Any gate claim rests on a run whose failures, if any,

**Rules 15-16 are NOT from that audit.** They were given by the user on 2026-08-27, after Phase 5.5

15. **A `PLAN.md` phase section that names work packages is the standing instruction to dispatch

16. **`phase-verifier` audits every phase handoff and every hotfix branch before the gate is

17. **Every release DoD, including hotfixes, ends with an own-eyes item before publish.** A hotfix

    `docs/evidence/phase-1/OWN-EYES.md` turned out to have been written by Claude at the user's

18. **A sweep or a redaction run that SKIPS any input reports the skip in its verdict line, and a
    skip fails the run unless it is acknowledged.** Silent skips are the fail-open class this
    repository has now hit three times, each time through a different door:
    - an EXTENSION ALLOW-LIST. `.log` was missing from the redactor's list, so two latency logs
      naming the developer's own cloud-sync service were counted as `skipped` - which reads exactly
      like a deliberate exclusion - and went through untouched.
    - a SELF-EXEMPTION. Run over its own directory the redactor rewrote its `IDENTITY` block to
      equal `SYNTHETIC` and carried on reporting success over a tree it was no longer scrubbing. The
      quieter half of the same run corrupted its foreign-slug table's keys, so six of the
      developer's other project names collapsed into one synthetic name - for the files processed
      after the corruption, and not for those before.
    - a REF THAT WAS NEVER WALKED. `git clone` brings other branches only as remote-tracking refs,

      twenty-one and finished cleanly saying so in a line nobody would read as a failure:
      "cloned: 355 commits, 1 branches".

    `--allow-skips` says the operator read the list; the sweep prints `identity=SKIPPED(<reason>)`
    rather than `identity=0` when it has no token file; and a rewrite states the ref count it
    actually touched. A count of zero is only evidence when something says what was looked at.

**Rules 19 and 20 were added on 2026-08-28**, after the `0.1.3` side-load packaging run. Rule 19 was
cited by the user by number before it existed here; it is written to match what was cited, and the
citation is recorded rather than quietly tidied away.

19. **An assertion about an ARTIFACT pins the exact set AND the exact count. Never a containment.**
    "The package contains what we expect" passes every single time this repository has actually been
    bitten — a stray root file, `docs/README.md` shipping as the user-facing README, a 38 KB mockup,
    a previous `.vsix` embedded in the next one. The defect class is *a file nobody meant to ship*,
    so the only assertion shape that can see it is equality over the whole listing. The count is
    pinned **beside** the set, not instead of it: a set comparison that is accidentally written
    against a filtered or empty listing passes vacuously, and a count is the cheapest thing that
    goes red when it does. Both legs, both names — `vsce ls` reports the ON-DISK names and the
    unzipped artifact reports the SHIPPED ones, and vsce renames between them
    (`LICENSE` → `extension/LICENSE.txt`, `README.md` → `extension/readme.md`,
    `CHANGELOG.md` → `extension/changelog.md`, everything else under `extension/`, plus
    `extension.vsixmanifest` and `[Content_Types].xml` which exist only in the zip). An audit
    written against one naming and run against the other matches nothing and reports a clean pass.

  Redaction and truncation must cover that path or previews silently miss content.
- **The PATCH COMPONENT IS NOT COMPARED, and widening the box is not the fix. Changed 2026-08-26 in
  the `v0.1.2` hotfix; the dated "Amendment 2026-08-26 — Version posture" section of
  `agent-deck-spec.md` is the authority.** `fingerprint.ts` anchors on `PINNED_CC_VERSION` and

  yourself widening it a third time, the answer is that the string is the wrong signal.
  **`PINNED_CC_VERSION` is a PROVENANCE anchor, not a support claim** — it names the release whose
  captured fixture proved the structure (`fixtures/cc-2.1.246/`), moves only with a harvest, and

- **A refusal fixture whose version quietly becomes acceptable does not fail. It passes, while
  testing nothing.** `synthetic-layout/07` and `08` have been re-versioned twice for exactly this:

- **Project-slug drive-letter case varies** on Windows (`c--Users-…` and `C--Users-…` both occur).

- **The `claude` on PATH cannot run at all, and the binary that writes the sessions lives inside the
  VS Code extension.** `claude --version` on PATH prints `Error: claude native binary not installed`

  which prints `2.1.246 (Claude Code)` as of 2026-08-26 and is what wrote `fixtures/cc-2.1.246/`.

  refused by this environment's command classifier; a scripted harvest goes through explicit
  `--allowedTools` plus `--add-dir`, with a fixed `--session-id` so the harvest cannot pick up the
  wrong file.
- **Fixtures must stay replayable without `~/.claude`.** `CLAUDE_PROJECTS_ROOT` overrides the live
  projects root; the negative control (no env var, fake HOME) must fail ENOENT rather than silently
  falling back.
- **Hooks are installed in the repo-local `.claude/settings.local.json`**, not `~/.claude`. That is
  deliberate and keeps G1 absolute — nothing under `~/.claude` is ever written. That file is
  committed and its hook block is **live**: every tool call in this repo POSTs to `127.0.0.1:47821`.
  The POST is unconditional, but `spike/hook-events-real.jsonl` (gitignored) only grows while a
  listener is actually bound — with nothing listening the POST takes ECONNREFUSED and appends
  nothing. Do not read a stable line count as evidence that hooks stopped firing.
- **CC's thinking blocks are empty on disk; the `signature` carries the bytes.** All 15 thinking
  blocks in the committed capture have an **empty `thinking` string** and a long populated
  `signature`. A G4 test asserting only that thinking *text* does not leak is therefore vacuous — it
  would pass forever while proving nothing. Redaction drops the `signature` field too, and the G4
  test asserts against the literal captured signature bytes.
- **CC's size labels are KiB, not KB.** The `<persisted-output>` stub reports a 63,774-byte payload
  as "62.3KB". Do not convert its numbers as decimal KB.
- **The `.gitattributes` rule marking fixtures as non-text is load-bearing.** `core.autocrlf=true` is set on this
  machine and there was no `.gitattributes` until Phase 1. Without that rule a fresh clone checks the
  fixtures out with CRLF endings, shifting every byte offset in every transcript — which breaks
  byte-exact tests on every machine except the one that captured the data, and looks like a parser
  bug rather than a checkout artifact. Verify by cloning and comparing bytes, never by inspecting the
  working tree you already have.
- **`git config core.longpaths true` is required, and it is repo-local.** Worktree creation fails
  outright with `Filename too long` otherwise — the fixture paths run ~150 characters and, added to a
  temp-rooted worktree, exceed Windows MAX_PATH. The same bites `git clone`: cloning into a deep
  directory fails **at checkout**, so pass `git -c core.longpaths=true clone` and clone somewhere
  short. "Replay from a clean checkout" is a DoD criterion, so this is not cosmetic — the repo works
  today partly because its own path happens to be short.
- **Subagents read a stale snapshot of `CLAUDE.md` and `git status`.** What a spawned agent sees is
  the state at the *parent session's* start, not at spawn time. Two `test-runner` runs in Phase 1
  confidently reported "CLAUDE.md documents RESOLVED 6" long after the file said 5, because they were
  quoting the injected snapshot rather than reading the file. When an agent reports a file's
  contents, verify against the file — and put facts an agent must act on in its prompt, not in
  CLAUDE.md.
- **A tracked test file contains a real NUL byte** (`src/parser/parse.test.ts`, deliberate fuzz
  input). Any `git log -p --all | grep …` audit must pass `-a`, or GNU grep abandons the stream and
  returns a clean-looking, meaningless result. This silently defeats the privacy residual check.
- **Implementer worktrees are cut from `main`, not the current branch.** A worker dispatched during a
  phase starts without that phase's merged work unless it first runs
  `git merge --ff-only <phase-branch>`. Put that instruction in every delegation prompt.
- **A subagent spawn briefly presents a sidecar with no transcript, and the fingerprint refuses the
  whole session for it.** CC writes `agent-<id>.meta.json` **before** `agent-<id>.jsonl` — measured
  at **+0.080 to +0.120 s across 5 of 5 spawns** in one real session. In that window
  `fingerprintSession` returns `subagentTranscriptMissing` and the session renders `unsupported`,
  with no tree, until the next successful graft. Reproduced against real session data; the same data
  intact returns `ok: true`, so **the refusal depends on when you looked, not on what is there**.
  `DEFAULT_DEBOUNCE_MS = 120` is the same order as the gap, so it is likely rather than rare. Do not
  "fix" this by deleting the check — that check is the tripwire for the subagent directory convention
  moving. See `PLAN.md` **Found in the field / F1**, which carries the measurements and the candidate
  shapes.

- **`vitest` and `tsc` disagree about duplicate imports, and vitest is the one that lies.**
  `esbuild` silently tolerates the same specifier imported twice; `tsc --noEmit` reports
  `TS2300 Duplicate identifier` and exits 2. A file can therefore be 54/54 green while
  `npm run typecheck` is broken, which is exactly how a "typecheck 0" claim reached a commit
  message in this repo. **A green test file is not a typecheck.**

- **`esbuild-svelte` does not propagate Svelte compiler warnings.** Measured both ways: removing
  a `svelte-ignore` and adding an unused CSS selector each produced `warnings: []`. Combined with
  the fact that no type checker covers `.svelte` and eslint does not lint them, "the component
  build is green" says very little. Do not treat a clean build as a check on component code.

- **`element.click()` throws on SVG elements in jsdom.** `HTMLElement.prototype.click` is not on
  `SVGElement`, and every canvas cell, dot and blob is SVG. Dispatch a `MouseEvent`;
  `webview/testkit.ts` exports `press` for this.

- **`toSessionState` in `src/model/graft.ts` has NO production callers** and sets neither
  `spawnEdges` nor `parked`. The production path is `SessionModel.viewFromSnapshot`. This is not
  cosmetic dead code: a worker reached for the obvious-looking function, got behaviour production
  never produces, and an entire decision was taken on the wrong premise before it was measured.
  Same class as `DataPathOptions.graft`.

- **The webview stage transform is a TRANSFORM, never a coordinate.** Pan and zoom on both the
  deck and the session interior are an SVG transform on a wrapper group. `layout.ts` stays a pure
  function of state, its goldens stay valid as numbers, and "a spawn adds, it never reflows"
  survives a user dragging the view around. An implementation that edited placements instead
  would break all three **silently** — `webview/store.test.ts` pans, zooms, then asserts
  `deckLayout` output is byte-identical, which is the test that catches the wrong shape.

- **Separation must use a CONSTANT footprint, not the drawn radius.** `cellRadius` grows with a
  cell's child count, so separating on it means one new tool call changes a radius, changes a
  collision, and MOVES A CELL ALREADY ON SCREEN. Measured: the incremental golden test failed
  immediately with `cell a69e0f453d5ca5f43 y moved`. `CELL_FOOTPRINT` is therefore fixed at
  `LABEL_PAD + CELL_RADIUS_MAX`, and a guard test asserts the literal agrees with the constant it
  was derived from.

- **The wide thing on the canvas is the TEXT, not the circle.** An agent label is ~26 characters
  at 15px — several hundred units — on a membrane of radius ~35. Separating on the membrane
  produced circles with clear space between them and labels written straight through each other,
  which reads to a user as "nothing was fixed". Cells separate on `LABEL_PAD`, and
  `LABEL_MAX_CHARS` is the single constant both the padding and the truncation derive from.

- **A stray file at the repo root escapes a `docs/**`-shaped `.vscodeignore` rule and ships.** A
  duplicate of the 38 KB design mockup was committed at the root by a scripted edit and went into
  the VSIX; `docs/ui/**` did not match it there. **The only way this class shows up is unzipping
  the artifact and listing it** — `npx vsce ls` — because the ignore file alone cannot answer
  "what does the package actually contain". Same family as the manifest/build disagreement that
  produced the inert `.js` host bundle.

- **Backticks inside a shell-quoted `node -e` are command substitution.** Writing generated source
  through `node -e "...\`Store.enterSession\`..."` let bash eat every backticked identifier and
  silently produce prose with holes in it — "both deck components now take , the constellation
  renders". It does not error. Write generated text through a **script file**, never a
  shell-quoted one-liner; the same rule the NUL-byte trap already taught.

- **`git commit -m "…"` is a shell-quoted string, so backticks inside it are command substitution.**
  The recorded `node -e` trap, on the one command every session runs. A message containing
  ``lands in `ignored` `` and ``the `atis` key`` committed as "lands in ." and "the  key" — no error,
  no warning, and the damage is only visible in `git log`. **Write commit messages through a file and
  `git commit -F <file>`**, with the file written by the Write tool.
- **`String.replace` TREATS $' IN THE REPLACEMENT AS "EVERYTHING AFTER THE MATCH",
  and it will silently duplicate a whole file.** JavaScript's
  `String.prototype.replace(needle, replacement)` honours $&, $`, $' and $$ in the
  REPLACEMENT even when the needle is a plain string, not a RegExp. A patch script whose
  replacement text quoted the shell fragment `grep -c $'\r$'`
  therefore spliced the remainder of the file back in at that point: **`HANDOVER.md` tripled and
  `CLAUDE.md` doubled**, on 2026-08-29, with no error and no warning. The only symptom was a
  section heading appearing three times, and `wc -l` looking too big - neither of which any test
  in this repository checks. Both files were rebuilt from git and re-applied with **slice-based**
  replacement (`t.slice(0,i) + replacement + t.slice(i+len)`), which has no substitution syntax
  at all. **Use slice, never `.replace()`, for document edits**, and probe a patched document by
  counting one of its own headings. Fourth member of the quoting-metacharacter family this file
  records - after the backtick in a shell-quoted `node -e`, the backtick in `git commit -m`, and
  the quoted heredoc - and the first where the tool doing the mangling is not a shell at all.

- **A quoted heredoc through the Bash tool is not reliably literal.** `python - <<'PY'` with
  `\\b` and `\\s` on the same regex line delivered `\b` (one backslash, which Python then read as a
  backspace) and `\\s` (two) — measured, same line, same heredoc. A patch script that matches source
  containing regex literals will silently find nothing. Use the Write tool for the script, or the
  Edit tool for the change; this is the same lesson as the backtick trap and the NUL-byte trap, and
  it is now three for three.
- **Source files in this working tree are CRLF; `fixtures/` is LF.** Measured across 315 tracked
  files: 150 CRLF / 152 LF / 8 no-newline, but outside `fixtures/` (which `.gitattributes` keeps LF
  deliberately) it is 150 CRLF to 10 LF — `src/` 50:1, `webview/` 61:2, root 18:1. Any scripted patch
  that reads a source file preserving newlines and matches on `\n`-joined text finds nothing.
  Normalise, patch, restore the original ending.
- **`grep -c $'\r' <file>` RETURNS 0 ON A CRLF FILE, and it is the check most likely to be
  reached for when verifying a scripted edit did not eat the line endings.** GNU grep strips a
  trailing CR before matching end-of-line, so the pattern never matches. Measured 2026-08-30 on a
  file that had just been rewritten: `grep -c` said **0** and `tr -cd '\r' | wc -c` said **97**,
  against 97 lines. The file was perfect and the check said it had been destroyed — the opposite
  failure to the usual one, and it would have sent the next reader rebuilding a correct file.
  **Count with `tr -cd`, and compare the CR count to the LF count.** This is the same grep
  behaviour the corrected CI guard already records, arriving through the other door: there it
  made a broken check look clean, here it makes a clean file look broken.

- **A quoted heredoc mangles `\r\n` as well as `\\`, and the damage is silent and mixed.**
  `python - <<'PY'` writing generated source delivered `\n` where the script said `\r\n`, so an
  inserted block was LF inside a file that is CRLF throughout, and separately turned `.split('\\n')`
  into a real newline inside a string literal. The second one at least fails loudly — esbuild
  says `Unterminated string literal` and points at the line. **The first one does not fail at
  all**: it produces a file that compiles, passes, and breaks the next scripted patch that reads
  it. Third measured instance of this trap after the `\\b`/`\\s` case. **Write the script with the
  Write tool.** And after any scripted edit, assert `CR == LF` on the whole file, which catches
  the silent half.

- **Do not assert fixture-set *sizes* in tests.** Counts hard-coded against the capture break on the
  next harvest and read as regressions. Derive them from the directory, or assert behaviour.

- **Subagent nesting is capped at 2 by this repo's own settings.** The same committed file sets
  `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH: "2"` (and `MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS: "6"`). That is why
  depth-2 is the deepest real data on disk and why any depth-3 proof had to be synthetic — raise the
  cap before expecting deeper trees from live capture.

- **A commit that both changes a file and describes that file's state will describe the *old* state.**
  This is the single most repeated defect in this repo's history, and Phase 2 committed it three
  times: a test count written just before two merges moved it, a "closed PASS 9/9" written while the
  verdict on record was `FAIL 8/9`, and a risk bullet saying a file "says nothing about X" in the very
  commit that made it say X. **Diff the two halves of your own commit against each other before
  committing.** Never write a live number or a verdict into a document from inside the phase that
  changes it — write what was verified and when.

- **The negative control needs `USERPROFILE` faked, not just `HOME`.** `spike/tail.mjs:28` resolves via
  `os.homedir()`, which reads `USERPROFILE` on Windows. Faking only `HOME` runs happily against the
  **real** `~/.claude` and reports `RESOLVED 36` — a green, confident, completely false pass on the one
  check whose entire purpose is proving we never touch it. Measured, not theorised.

- **`fixtures/hook-events/` is content-free, not anonymous.** Its redaction destroys values but
  deliberately keeps `cwd`, `transcript_path`, `session_id`, `agent_id` and `prompt_id` verbatim,
  because a fixture without them cannot pin the main-thread rule. Paths are backslash-separated
  (`C:\Users\dev\…`) — a privacy sweep greping a forward-slash form finds nothing. Phase 5 must
  cover this directory explicitly.

- **The spike audit fails loudly on a wrong `--project` path — it exits 2, not 0.** An earlier claim
  that it "exits 0 as a silent pass" was false and propagated through an entire phase because it had
  been written into the `phase-verifier`'s memory store by the orchestrator. **Nothing in
  `.claude/agent-memory/` is ground truth** — it is a claim to re-measure, and the party being judged
  must not write there.

- **`"type": "module"` + a CommonJS bundle named `.js` = an extension that silently does not
  activate.** Node resolves a `.js` file's format from the nearest `package.json`, so VS Code parses
  the CJS host bundle as ESM and `module.exports` never reaches it. It does **not throw** — you get
  `activate = undefined` and an inert extension that still builds and still packages. Measured against
  the unzipped VSIX both ways. The host bundle is therefore `dist/extension.cjs`, and
  `src/extension.test.ts` loads whatever path `main` actually names and asserts `activate` is a
  function. **The defect class is "the manifest and the build disagree" and it will recur** — that
  test is the guard, not the naming convention.

- **The truncation marker under-reports at the shipped default.** **Every** payload over 8,192 bytes
  is cut twice — inline ones included, so do not go looking only at the offload path: of the 8
  affected payloads in the capture, **7 never touch `tool-results/`**. `redact` cuts at 8192 and
  appends a correct marker (making the string 8,248 bytes), then the grafter's `preview()` re-cuts
  *that* and re-marks against the length it received. At `previewBytes=8192` all 8 claim
  "8192 of 8248" when the originals run to 63,774 — the marker under-reports the largest by 7.73×.
  `redact.ts` tells callers to budget for the marker; `preview()` does not. Also means
  `agentDeck.previewBytes` above 8192 cannot increase kept bytes. **Phase 4 item, recorded in
  `PLAN.md` with the measurements — do not re-derive it from scratch.**

- **Never write a raw control character into source.** A worker wrote a NUL-injection guard with a
  literal `0x00` byte instead of a backslash-zero escape. The file became **binary to git** — no reviewable diff ever
  again — and it compounds the documented `grep -a` hazard that already costs this repo a trap. Fixing
  the encoding also revealed the guard had never been tested at all. Escapes, always.

- **A module-boundary partition produces silent seams, not crashes.** Phase 3's host emitted
  `<div id="app">` while the webview looked for `#agent-deck-root` and fell back to `document.body`.
  Both packages were internally consistent, both fully tested, and they disagreed — the panel rendered
  into the wrong element and nothing failed. Two agreeing literals is not a contract;
  `src/bridge/contract.ts` holds the single definition. **When you split work by file ownership,
  the bugs land between the files, so mutate the hand-off line rather than the implementation.**

- **A shebang in a `.mjs` file breaks vitest collection — but only in a CRLF checkout.** vite strips
  it with `hashbangRE = /^#!.*\n/`, and JavaScript's `.` does not match `\r`, so the pattern matches
  the LF form and not the CRLF one. `.gitattributes` `text=auto` plus `core.autocrlf=true` means the
  author's working tree holds LF and a fresh checkout holds CRLF: the file imports fine for whoever
  wrote it and throws `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token` for everyone else. Measured on
  `scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs`; removing the shebang is the fix (nothing here is exec'd directly).
  **This is the fixtures lesson applying to SOURCE** — "verify by cloning and comparing bytes, never
  by inspecting the working tree you already have" is not only about fixtures.

- **A suite that fails to COLLECT reports as "skipped", which reads green in the summary line.**
  When the above fired, `src/release/privacy.test.ts` printed `24 skipped` and **zero** of its
  assertions ran; the totals line looked healthy. Read the skip count and **account for every skip by
  GATE, not against a number.** An earlier version of this bullet said "exactly one deliberate skip
  (`AGENT_DECK_PACKAGE_AUDIT=1`), so any other skip is a defect" — that was measuring this machine,
  not the repo. **There are SEVEN environment-conditional gates as of 2026-09-04** — it said four
  until 2026-08-28, six until Phase 7, and **six again in this bullet until a `phase-verifier`
  re-counted them at the Phase 4 gate and found seven.** That is three corrections to the same
  number, which is the actual lesson: *the count is a census over the tree and it moves whenever a
  gate is added, so re-derive it rather than quoting this sentence.* Today:
  `runIf(AGENT_DECK_PACKAGE_AUDIT === '1')` (`src/release/vsix.test.ts`, twice — the second added
  with the junction-door suites), `skipIf(!WSL.usable)` twice (`src/model/pathmatrix.test.ts`),
  and three in `src/release/readme.test.ts` (`skipIf(LIVE_SETTINGS === null)` plus
  `describe.skipIf(SPEC === null)` twice). Six of them are live on the dev
  box, which is why the observed count is 1; on a runner without WSL the healthy count is ~7, and on
  one where `SPEC === null` too it is ~11 - the
  old rule would call them defects. A guard against an import failure must not itself import the
  broken module:
  `privacy.test.ts` reads the script's first two bytes with `fs` for exactly that reason.

- **The spike audit is NOT a CRLF regression guard, and believing it was is why one existed nowhere.**
  Measured twice: converting the fixture `.jsonl` files (124 CRs), and then all 13 files under
  `fixtures/cc-2.1.234/projects` (**1,600 CRs**), both left the audit's output byte-identical at
  exit 0 — the reader splits on LF and `JSON.parse` treats a trailing `\r` as whitespace. The
  `.gitattributes` rule is still load-bearing for byte-offset tests; the thing that actually checks
  it is the Node byte-scan step in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (`files containing CR: 0`).

- **`vsce` RENAMES the licence inside the artifact: `LICENSE` on disk becomes `extension/LICENSE.txt`
  in the zip.** `vsce ls` reports the on-disk name, so an audit written against the packager's own
  listing looks for a file that is not there and reports a clean pass. Same family as every other
  "only the unzipped artifact knows what shipped" finding here.

- **`dist/` in `.vscodeignore` is an ALLOW-LIST, and must stay one.** `dist/` is shipped wholesale,
  so every stray emit ships: the theater bundle, a previous `.vsix`, source maps, and — measured in
  Phase 5 — `webview/wire.test.ts` and `webview/capture.test.ts`, which both `mkdtemp` **inside**
  `dist/` deliberately (they write nothing outside the repo). `vsce ls` enumerated
  `dist/wire-test-<random>/**` as packaged content during a real run. The rule is therefore
  `dist/**` denied with three `!` re-admissions, in that order. Do not go back to denying scratch
  directories by name — that is the `docs/**`-shaped rule that already failed once.

- **`src/parser/parse.test.ts` contains exactly ONE NUL byte, not 884.** The 884 figure appears in
  `HANDOVER.md` and is wrong: counted across all 698 blobs reachable from every ref, three contain
  any NUL and each contains one byte. The `grep -a` hazard is real and unchanged — GNU grep still
  abandons the stream — only the number was inflated.

- **`engines.node` was a lie for four phases, and only CI could say so.** It declared `>=20` while
  `jsdom@30` requires `^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0` and its transitive `undici@8` requires
  `>=22.19.0`. `actions/setup-node` honours the manifest, installed Node 20, and the suite died on
  `webidl.util.markAsUncloneable is not a function`. It could never reproduce locally: this machine
  runs 24.15.0, exactly on jsdom's floor. **A declared floor nobody runs on is a claim, not a
  constraint** - `src/release/workflow.test.ts` now derives it from `node_modules` and compares.
  Watch for it after any dependency bump.

- **libuv ABORTS the process when a watched path has an 8.3 short component.**
  `Assertion failed: !_wcsnicmp(filename, dir, dirlen), file src\win\fs-event.c, line 72`. GitHub's
  Windows runners return `C:\Users\RUNNER~1\AppData\Local\Temp` from `os.tmpdir()`, and
  `src/watch/watcher.test.ts:47` / `src/watch/inference.test.ts:40` point a real `fs.watch` at a
  `mkdtemp` under it. There is **no failing assertion to read** - the process dies ~1 s in with no
  summary line. CI works around it by pointing `TMP`/`TEMP` at `RUNNER_TEMP`; the actual fix is
  `realpathSync.native()` before watching, and it would protect any Windows dev whose `TEMP` is
  short-named.

- **`actions/checkout` defaults to `fetch-depth: 1`, which silently guts any history-scanning
  check.** `scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs` would have printed `VERDICT PASS unexpected=0 secrets=0
  foreign=0` over a history that was not there - a clean result from an absent corpus, on the gate
  for a public flip. It surfaced only because `privacy.test.ts` asserts the history leg covers more
  bytes than the working tree rather than trusting the verdict. Any CI that sweeps needs
  `fetch-depth: 0`.

- **The `runner` context is NOT available in a job-level `env:`** (only github/needs/strategy/
  matrix/vars/secrets/inputs). Using it makes the workflow unparseable, and the diagnostic is close
  to nothing: "This run likely failed because of a workflow file issue", 0s duration, no log, no
  annotated line. Set it through `$GITHUB_ENV` in a step instead. Note what did not catch it:
  `src/release/workflow.test.ts` asserts structure without a YAML parser and cannot evaluate Actions
  context rules - it stayed green at 32 passed through a workflow GitHub refused to run.

- **`vsce ls` reports files that EXIST, so any assertion on it depends on build state.** A cold
  checkout has no `dist/`, and `src/extension.test.ts` / `src/hooks/egress.test.ts` build the HOST
  bundle mid-run as a side effect while nothing builds the webview one - so an exact-set assertion
  silently depended on test ORDER. `src/release/vsix.test.ts` now builds what is missing first.

- **An expensive subprocess called once per test is a test that passes or fails by CPU load.**
  `src/release/vsix.test.ts` spawned `vsce ls` **six times**, once per test, uncached, under vitest's
  **5 s default** timeout - and each spawn measures 1.4-3.2 s. It was green run alone and red in the
  full suite. (The aside here blamed `src/perf/perf.test.ts` running concurrently and saturating the
  machine. After Phase 5 that explanation is doubtful — see the superseded `tailPoll` bullet below —
  but this finding stands on its own measurements, which are about uncached subprocess spawns under
  a 5 s default timeout, not about the perf file.) Measured
  in Phase 6; the fix is memoising the listing at module scope and warming it inside the `beforeAll`
  that already owns a 120 s budget, which also cut the file from ~13 s of subprocess time to ~1.3 s.
   **The diagnosis rule matters more than the fix:** a suite failure that disappears on a second run
   is a defect report about the test, not noise to re-roll. Re-running the suite to "see if it was
   flaky" is how this survived four phases. Same family as the note above that `vsce ls` reports files
   that EXIST and so depended on test ORDER - that one was build state, this one is wall-clock, and
   both come from treating an environment-sensitive subprocess as if it were a pure function.

- **The observed engines' own state directories are a local-tooling-ships class member you cannot
  guess in advance.** opencode keeps per-project state in `.opencode/` at the repo root — with its
  own `node_modules/` — and it accumulated untracked until it shipped in the VSIX. The Phase 5
  exact-set guard caught it: `77f964f` denies `.opencode/**` (and the root `AGENTS.md`) in
  `.vscodeignore`, and `.gitignore` gives `.opencode/` the documented `.claude/` treatment. Same
  family as the `docs/**`-shaped mockup finding: any per-tooling directory the tools under
  observation write into the repo root is a packaging hazard until it is named, and each new
  engine adds a new one.
- **The `package-lock.json` root duplicates the manifest's `engines`/license, and release work can
  leave them apart.** After the flip, the committed lock still carried the pre-flip manifest
  (`node >=20`, `vscode ^1.90.0`, `UNLICENSED`) while `package.json` said `>=22.22.2` /
  `^1.75.0` / `MIT`. Regenerate the lock in the same commit as any manifest
  `engines`/license change and diff the two halves of the commit against each other — the usual
  rule, applied to a pair of files that look unrelated.
- **THE MID-RUN DEATH HAS ONE EXIT CODE, NOT TWO, AND `127` IS NOT IT.** Both bullets that used to
  sit here are superseded by v0.7.0 Phase 1c (2026-09-07/08), and they were wrong in the same way:
  they recorded *"exit 127 at ~19/40 files (Phase 5) and `-1073740791` (`0xC0000409`) at ~6/40
  (Phase 7): same class, different code"*, and called `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run`
  **the fix** — which it never was, because there was nothing about the command to fix.

  **`127` is what Git Bash prints when Windows terminates the process.** A POSIX wait status has
  eight bits for an exit code and every Windows abnormal-termination status has its high bit set,
  so the shell collapses all of them onto one number and the status that names the fault is gone
  before it reaches the scrollback. Measured, one `node -e "process.exitCode = N"` per row: 0–255
  render as themselves, 256/383/384 as 0/**127**/128, every negative as **127**, and
  **`0xC0000409` (3221226505) as 127**. `cmd.exe` and PowerShell hand the code through unchanged
  and **cannot produce 127 at all** — cmd's "not recognized" is 1. Nothing in npm or vitest emits
  127 anywhere.

  **So the two "classes" in the ledger were one fault seen through two shells**, and the ledger's
  own data already said so: every run recorded through `scripts/test-run.mjs` (which spawns via
  `ComSpec`, i.e. `cmd.exe`) reported `3221226505` and never 127; every ad-hoc gate run typed at a
  Git Bash prompt reported 127 and never a raw status. **Phase 1c then captured it 12 times in 92
  runs across five trees — ~13%, every one `0xC0000409`, including at the commit before any Phase
  1c code existed.** Always early (3.1–17.5 s), never a summary line, never anything on stderr but
  the two `npm notice` lines.

  **What to do:** take gate runs through `scripts/test-run.mjs`, which records the raw code and
  classifies it; run `node scripts/test-run.mjs --explain <code>` when you find one in a
  scrollback. Never reason from a `$?` of 127 — it is the erasure of the answer, not the answer.
  Switching commands is not a remedy and never was. **The cause of the fail-fast is NOT
  established** and this bullet does not pretend otherwise; `lab/docs/evidence/v0.7.0/phase-1c/FINDINGS.md`
  and the runner ledger carry the whole record.
- **The handoff skill says to check the phase-verifier's agent memory into version control; the
  repo gitignores ALL of `.claude/` (0 tracked files) by its privacy treatment.** The memory at
  `.claude/agent-memory/phase-verifier/` persists locally only. Forcing it into version control
  in a public repo is a privacy decision, not a hygiene step — the repo's treatment of local
  tooling state is the stronger rule.

- **The `claude`-on-PATH trap has a SECOND ENGINE, and it broke mid-session.** `opencode` on
  `PATH` is an npm shim (`%APPDATA%/npm/opencode`) that reports *"opencode-ai's postinstall script
  was not run"* while the real binary is perfectly fine. Measured on 2026-08-26: `opencode
  --version` returned `1.18.22` at 18:2x and the shim was broken by 18:58, because **OpenCode had
  self-updated to `1.18.23` underneath it**. The real binary is
  `%APPDATA%/npm/node_modules/opencode-ai/node_modules/opencode-windows-x64/bin/` — invoke that
  from any probe or harvest. Two consequences beyond the path: a control run is mandatory (the
  first XDG_DATA_HOME measurement looked like a behaviour change and was the shim failing in
  BOTH arms), and **a binary's version number can change while you are measuring it** — the DB
  held `1.18.21` and `1.18.22` sessions while the binary went `1.18.22` → `1.18.23`. Anchor on
  the fixture's `session.version`, never on the binary's.

- **WAL FILE SIZE IS NOT A WRITE INDICATOR, and a control keyed on it rejects good runs.**
  `opencode.db-wal` measured **exactly 4,181,832 bytes across 2 h 30 m and four separate probes**
  while `opencode.db` grew 425 KB and the event table gained 116 rows. SQLite reuses WAL frames
  in place; the file rests at its high-water mark and never tracks writes. The Phase 2 hot-WAL
  probe's vacuity control was built on it and would have reported "this run proves nothing" on
  every correct run forever — the expensive direction, whose only symptom is the user re-running
  a good measurement. Key such a control on the **event counter, `max(seq)`, or the main database
  file's size**. Same family as the already-recorded rule that a failure which disappears on
  re-run is a defect report about the check, not noise.

- **A newly tracked top-level directory is outside the privacy sweep until it is NAMED, and the
  sweep will not tell you.** Phase 2 tracked `.vscode/` (this repo had none, so "press F5" was
  never actually available) and `node scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs` kept returning `VERDICT PASS
  unexpected=0 secrets=0 foreign=0` exit 0 on every run — because the sweep reports on the corpus
  it was told about. What caught it was the separate completeness assertion in
  `src/release/privacy.test.ts` ("covers every tracked top-level directory"), on the first FULL
  suite run. **Third time that guard has caught this class**; its own comment records `media/`.
  When it fires, regenerate `docs/evidence/privacy/report.json` **after** committing the
  `CAPTURE_CORPORA` change — the head-freshness test asserts the script has not moved since the
  recorded head, so a report generated first names a head the change came after.

- **SQLite `LIKE` is CASE-INSENSITIVE for ASCII, and it will hand you a confident wrong answer.**
  **Any needle, secret or G8 check over a SQLite corpus must use `GLOB` or `instr()`** — the same
  family as the `grep -a` trap, reached through a different tool. Measured on the anchor corpus,
  `LIKE` → `GLOB`: the foreign project name **69 → 0** (it was matching `ov`+`erw`+`rite`),
  `ACCESS_TOKEN` **10 → 0** and `github_pat` **9 → 0** (both were matching this repo's own prose
  about `access_token` columns). **But `api_key` is 21 → 14 and `password` is 17 → 17: `GLOB` is
  not a synonym for zero.** Those survivors are benign *today* — they are OpenCode's own docs
  (`OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD=your-password`) and this repo's sessions quoting
  `privacy-sweep.mjs`'s own needle list — and `secrets=0` is still correct because the sweep keys
  on high-entropy **assignment shape**, not on the bare word. **Do not read a non-zero `GLOB`
  count as a breach, and do not read zero as the expected answer**; an earlier version of this
  bullet claimed "zero, every one", which was false and would have sent the next reader escalating
  on 17 hits of the word `password`. Nothing pins these to prose, so re-measure rather than assume.

- **A `beforeAll` that shells out has vitest's 10 s DEFAULT hookTimeout, and when it loses the race
  the failure reports as SKIPS with a clean-looking tests line.** The `G5 dependency review` hook in
  `src/hooks/egress.test.ts` ran esbuild with no timeout argument; Phase 3's added suite weight pushed it over, and
  the summary read `1570 passed | 7 skipped` with **no failed-test count at all**, because a
  suite-level failure contributes none. Six G5 zero-egress assertions ran zero times. The sibling
